0.a: Pupils walk around, wave and say Hello! or Hi! to three classmates, then all face a flag drawn on the board, wave and shout Hello, Oman! together.
Pupils trace waves in the air from left to right with a 'pencil finger' as a dhow sails on Oman's sea, then wave and say Goodbye, Fatma! Goodbye, Sami!

1.a: Pupils sit in a circle like guests in an Omani majlis; each asks the next pupil What's your name? and hears My name's … / I'm …, then offers a pretend date with a smile.
The teacher mimes a boy, a girl, a cat or a friend and pupils shout the word; for friend, pairs shake hands and say Hello, friend! warmly, as Omanis greet guests.

2.a: One pupil closes his/her eyes; a classmate says Hello! My name's … in a funny voice and the pupil guesses the name; the class claps politely to show respect for every friend.
Pupils stand one by one, put a hand on the heart and say Hello. My name's … I'm from Oman!; the class answers Well done! with a big clap.

3.a: The teacher says mum, dad, brother or sister and pupils mime that person helping at home, such as pouring Omani coffee for guests, then freeze when the teacher claps.
A pupil mimes a helpful job, like carrying a basket of dates or sweeping the yard; the class guesses Mum? Dad? Brother? Sister? and the pupil points to the story picture.
Pupils tap their desks for words that start with /t/ (tree, teddy, toys, train) and stay still for other words; the last word is tower: pupils make a tall Omani fort tower with their arms.

4.a: Groups freeze like a family photo on National Day; the teacher points and asks Who's this? and the group answers This is my mum / dad / brother / sister.
Pupils pass a family flashcard while humming the song; on Stop! the holder answers Who's this? – This is my …; for grandpa or grandma, all bow a little to show respect for elders, as in Oman.
Pupils jump up like popcorn for /p/ words (pen, pie, pin, pink) and sit for others; the last word is palm: everyone sways like a date palm, a famous tree of Oman.

5.a: Pairs make their finger puppets meet at a pretend souq stall: Hello! What's your name? – My name's Sami. Who's this? – This is Meg. Then the puppets say Goodbye!
The teacher says n words and pupils mime them: night (sleep), nest (a bird sits), nut (crack it), nose (touch it); for night, they look up at the stars in Oman's clear desert sky.

6.a: Four pupils hold family flashcards and stand like a family; the class asks Who's this? and each answers This is my …; then the 'family' waves a pretend Omani flag together.
Groups make the letters s, a, t, p, n with their bodies and the class says the sound; the last letter is s: pupils wave their arms like the sea and say s-s-sea, where Omani dhows sail.
The teacher says sounds (t-a-p, n-a-p, p-a-t); pupils blend the word and act it; for tap, they mime turning off the tap to save water, which is precious in Oman.

7.a: The teacher names people (mum, my friend Sami, sister); pupils hug themselves for family and high-five a neighbour for friend, then shake hands with a classmate like kind Omani neighbours.
A pupil mimes a Unit 1 word (cat, mum, boy, sister) and the class guesses; the teacher's last mime is a boy putting on a kumma, the Omani cap, and pupils shout Boy!
Pairs pretend their desk is the sand of an Omani beach: one 'writes' s, a, t, p or n with a finger and the partner says the sound, then they swap.

8.a: The teacher says Show me a ruler! and pupils hold it up and say It's a ruler; for the last round, pupils lend a pen to a friend and say Here you are, sharing kindly as Omanis do.
Pairs play shopkeeper and child at an Omani souq: the child points to a school thing, the shopkeeper says It's a pen! / It's an eraser!, and both say Thank you! politely.

9.a: Pupils pass a bag round the circle; whoever holds it takes out an object and says I've got a ruler / an eraser; the last pupil points to the flag on the board and says I've got a flag!
A pupil draws a school thing in the air and the class guesses It's a pen!; the pupil answers Yes! I've got a pen; the teacher's last drawing is an Omani coffee pot for welcoming guests.

10.a: The teacher says book, crayon, pencil or pencil case and pupils mime putting it carefully in their bags; the teacher adds: we look after our books, a gift to every child in Oman.
The teacher holds up a 'found' crayon, pencil or book; the owner says It's my crayon!, collects it and says Thank you; the teacher praises honesty: in Oman we return what we find.

11.a: Each pupil holds one object; the teacher calls a word and holders stand and say I've got a book!, others say I haven't got a book!; last round: all hold hands and say I've got a friend!
The class pretends to pack for a school trip to a wadi; the teacher calls things and pupils say I've got a pencil! or I haven't got a crayon!, then promise to keep the wadi clean.
Pupils fly a pretend kite for words starting with /k/ (king, kite, cloud, cut) and stay still for others; the last word is camel: everyone rides like a camel in the Omani desert.

12.a: Pairs show their paper bags: I've got a pen. I haven't got a ruler.; the partner offers the missing thing and says Here you are!, showing Omani generosity.

13.a: Teams race to draw the school thing the teacher says (bag, pen, crayon, ruler) and say It's a …; the last drawing is a bag with the Omani flag and pupils name its colours.
The teacher sounds out h-a-t, c-a-t and m-a-p; pupils blend and mime each word; for hat, they put on a pretend kumma, the cap Omani men and boys wear.

14.a: Two pupils each hold up two school things; the class says Same! or Different! and names the different thing; the teacher ends: We are different, but we are all friends in Oman.
The teacher gives orders like Point to the pen, please!; pupils point and name the object only when they hear please, because in Oman we always say please and thank you.
Pupils freeze in the shapes of i, m, h, c and r and the class says the sound; the last letter is m for mountain: pupils stand tall like the Al Hajar Mountains of Oman.

15.a: The teacher draws one to six dates on a palm tree on the board; pupils count on their fingers and say the number, then name the colours: brown dates, green leaves.
The teacher calls a colour and pupils touch something of that colour and count to six with a partner; the last colours are red and green, two colours of the Omani flag.

16.a: Pupils walk and ask three friends How old are you? – I'm six!, then count the friends on their fingers and clap six times together like a happy Omani drum beat.
The teacher says a number and a colour (five, red); pupils write the number in the air with a big arm; last: Draw a flag! and pupils air-draw the Omani flag and wave it.

17.a: The teacher says Touch the door! Point to the window! Look at the whiteboard!; at the door, pupils pretend to open it with a smile and say Welcome!, like an Omani home welcoming guests.
The teacher says I spy … and pupils point and say It's a window / door / whiteboard / teacher!; at the end everyone waves to thank the people who keep our school clean.
Pupils swim like fish for /f/ words (four, five, fan, fork, fin) and freeze for others; the last word is fish: they pull a net like Omani fishermen.

18.a: The teacher slowly draws a door, a window, then a fort; pupils ask What's this? and answer It's a door!; the last answer is It's a fort!, like the old forts of Oman.
Pupils walk; on Clap! they touch the nearest object and a partner asks What's this? – It's a door!; the teacher draws a carved door: an old Omani door with beautiful carving.
Pupils wiggle their arms like an octopus for words starting with /ɒ/ (on, octopus, ox, olive) and stand still for others; then all 'swim' in the Sea of Oman.

19.a: The teacher says Put the pen on the desk! Put the bag under the chair! Put the book in the bag!; pupils do it quickly; last: Put the paper in the bin! – we keep Oman tidy.
The teacher says The bottle is on the sand! The bag is under the rock!; pupils mime picking up the rubbish at an Omani beach and putting it in the bin, then cheer.
Pupils climb like goats on Oman's mountains for words starting with /g/ (gate, grapes, goat, girl) and sit down for others; the last word is fig.

20.a: A pupil hides a paper date in, on or under something; the class guesses It's under the chair! / It's in the bag! until they find it; dates are a famous Omani fruit.
Pupils make a palm tree with one arm; the teacher says The bird is in the tree. The dates are on the tree. The cat is under the tree.; pupils show it with the other hand.
Pupils whisper shh and tiptoe for /ʃ/ words (shell, shop, shed, ship) and freeze for others; the last word is ship: they row together like sailors on an old Omani ship.

21.a: Pupils show their desk tidies like craftspeople at an Omani craft souq; a 'visitor' asks What's this? and the maker answers It's a desk tidy. I've got a pen in it.
Pupils bounce a pretend ball for /b/ words (bird, boy, ball, book) and freeze for others; the last word is Bahla: pupils build a fort wall with their arms like Bahla Fort.

22.a: The teacher names classroom things and groups make them with their bodies (an open door, a window, a desk); last: Make a majlis! – groups sit in a circle and welcome a guest.
The teacher says I spy something beginning with /b/ and pupils name it (bag, book, ball); the last one is /f/: the flag of Oman, drawn on the board.
The teacher plays a fish seller at Muttrah fish market and calls sounds (f-i-sh, sh-o-p, b-i-n, sh-e-d); pupils blend and shout the word to 'buy' it.
Three corners are people, things and places; the teacher says a word and pupils point to its corner; the last word is Muscat and pupils say Muscat is our capital!

23.a: A pupil is a guide for a visitor to the class: This is the door. Where's the bag? It's on the desk. The visitor says Thank you!, enjoying Omani hospitality.
Pupils hold up a school thing and say its colour (It's a green pencil!), then the class makes a long line of things: red, white, then green, like the Omani flag.
The teacher says three words and pupils jump at the one with a different first sound; the last set is fish, fan, dhow: pupils find dhow and sail like an Omani dhow.
Teams take turns: the teacher says a sound and the team gives a word for it; a team gets a bonus star for an Omani word, such as s – souq, d – dates or f – fort.

24.a: Pupils drive pretend cars in a National Day parade; the teacher asks What colour is it? and pupils answer It's a red car! / It's a green car! as they decorate them with flags.
A pupil mimes playing with a ball, car, robot or teddy and the class guesses; the pupil passes the pretend toy to a friend and says Your turn!, playing fairly as good Omani friends do.

25.a: The teacher shows toy cards and asks What colour is it?; pupils answer It's blue!; if the colour is red, white or green, a colour of the Omani flag, they clap twice.
Pupils become toys (robots walk, balls bounce, teddies hug); on Freeze! the teacher asks What colour is it?; then the robots help tidy the classroom, helping others like good citizens.

26.a: The class flies a pretend plane to Muscat, Salalah and Sur; at each stop pupils share a toy with a friend: Here's my yo-yo! / Here's my train!
Pupils pass a pretend plate of dates round the class; each says I'm sharing! and offers it to a friend, who says Thank you!, like Omani families welcoming guests.

27.a: Pupils ask three friends What's your favourite toy? – It's my train!; then they guess the teacher's: It's my toy dhow, a boat of Oman!
In groups, a pupil mimes playing with a favourite toy and the group asks What's your favourite toy? and guesses It's your yo-yo!; the teacher's last mime is flying a kite on an Omani beach.
Pupils lift a pretend ladder for /l/ words (leaf, ladder, lemon, lamp) and freeze for others; the last word is lime: they dry limes in the sun, as Omani families do for cooking.

28.a: Pairs pretend it is Eid and give a paper toy as a gift: This is a car. It's blue. It's my favourite!; the partner says Thank you! and shares a toy back.

29.a: Pupils ride pretend toy camels in a camel race, a popular Omani sport; the teacher asks What colour is your camel? and pupils answer It's brown! It's my favourite!
Pupils drive a pretend van for /v/ words (village, vet, vase, van) and stop for others; the van visits an old mountain village in Oman and pupils wave hello.

30.a: A pupil sits in the hot seat as a visitor; the class asks What's your name? How old are you? What's your favourite toy?, then everyone says Welcome to Oman!
Pairs act as a toy seller and buyer at a National Day fair: What's this? – It's my robot. It's yellow!; the buyer says Thank you! and both wave pretend flags.
The teacher says a word (sun, dad, log, chin, van, dates); pupils say the first sound and mime it; for dates, they pretend to eat a sweet Omani date.

31.a: The teacher draws simple outlines: a fort door, a flag, a dhow's sail, a round coffee cup; pupils call out rectangle, triangle, circle or square for each one.

32.a: The teacher draws one camel or many camels, one ball or many balls; pupils ask What's this? – It's a camel! or What are these? – They're camels!, then share their toy cards.

0.a: Groups mime a type of media (newspaper, blog, TV, magazine, radio) and the class guesses; for the last round, the mime must show news about a place in Oman, such as Wahiba Sands.

1.a: Pairs suggest a screen-free activity in Oman using screen time, excessive and addicted (Instead of excessive screen time, I'd hike in Wadi Shab); the class votes for the best plan.
Students move to Agree / Disagree corners for fun screen-time statements and give a reason and an example; the last statement is: Omani families should keep one screen-free meal a day.

2.a: Groups compare two Omani places of their choice (Nizwa and Sur, Salalah and Muscat) using more … than, the most and as … as; the class votes for the funniest true comparison.
A student gives clues with not as … as and as … as (It's not as big as Muscat, but it's as famous as Nizwa); the class guesses the Omani town or place.
Groups mime a phrasal verb (pick up, look after, turn off, clean up) in a short scene about caring for Oman, like picking up litter on a beach; the class guesses the verb.

3.a: Each team writes one true and one fake headline about life in Oman; other teams decide which is fake, using source, trust, reporter and fake news to explain.
A student picks a prompt, e.g. Omani teens should get news online, not from newspapers, and gives an opinion with a reason and an example in 30 seconds, stressing key words.

4.a: Students form a human pie chart of the class's favourite Omani dish (shuwa, harees, majboos); pairs describe it: The most popular dish is …, the least popular is ….
The teacher sketches a column chart of the class's favourite sport to watch in Oman as hands go up; pairs race to say one correct describing or comparing sentence about it.
Drafts move round the group; each student adds one star comment and one wish, using respectful words, then the writer thanks them, showing the Omani value of respect.

5.a: Groups have 30 seconds to pitch their blog's name, audience and colours on an Omani topic (Omani food, wadi adventures); the class votes with claps.
Each group writes a catchy headline for a future blog post about young people and Oman Vision 2040 (e.g. Young Omanis Go Digital); groups read them aloud and vote.

6.a: The class builds a funny story about a trip to Jebel Akhdar, one sentence each, using a phrasal verb or a comparison (We set off early. The road was steeper than …).

7.a: Students mime drought, floods, heat waves or a rising sea level and the class guesses; then the actor says one sentence about protecting Oman's environment using threat or climate change.

8.a: Volunteers stand in a line and raise their arms higher to show a rising trend; the class narrates it with chart language, then says one small action to keep Oman green.
Groups play roles (family, school, factory, government) and each says one promise to protect Oman's environment using new words (We will release less …, We will reduce fossil fuels).

9.a: One student says a cause about life in Oman (Because of heavy rain, …) and the next completes the effect (the wadis flow); the chain continues using different connectors.
Pairs predict the future with connectors: Due to more tree planting, Muscat will be greener.; the class claps for the most hopeful and correct prediction.
Teams race to make compound nouns linked to Oman (date palm, seafood, fish market, coffee pot, sunrise, sandstorm) and say which type each one is.

10.a: Pairs create a 10-second radio advert for an eco-friendly product made in Oman, using two words such as emission, consumer, eco-friendly or regulate; they perform it.
Pairs debate for 30 seconds each: Plastic bags should not be used in Omani souqs; they use We believe that… / I see your point, but… and stress the important words.

11.a: Groups plan a plastic-free picnic on an Omani beach and give three ideas with reasons; the class picks the most creative plan.
Three students say a topic sentence, a supporting sentence and a concluding sentence about why we should protect turtles at Ras Al Jinz; the class checks the order and claps.
Teams 'bid' pretend money on topic sentences the teacher reads about keeping Oman's wadis clean; strong sentences are worth buying, weak ones are not; the richest team wins.

12.a: Teams create a catchy slogan for an eco-friendly bag inspired by Omani heritage, such as a dhow or frankincense pattern; teams read them aloud and vote.
Each team has 30 seconds to sell its reusable bag to the class, acting as sellers in Muttrah Souq; shoppers 'buy' with pretend coins and give one piece of feedback.

13.a: A student describes a unit word without saying it (drought, greenhouse gas, therefore) and the team guesses; the last word must link to Oman, such as sea level for its long coast.

14.a: Pairs decide which renewable energy suits Oman best (solar, wind, hydro) and give one reason; pairs share and the class votes with raised hands.

15.a: Pairs turn an informal invitation (Hi, come to my house!) into a formal one inviting a guest to try Omani coffee and dates; they read both in fun voices.
Teams build compound nouns from energy words (solar panel, wind farm, power station) and use one in a sentence about Oman in the future and Vision 2040.

16.a: Groups describe an eco-friendly stadium for Oman in four sentences using also, so, because and but; the class votes for the best design.
One student states an idea about a solar-powered school in Oman; the partner continues with the connector the teacher calls (however, moreover, therefore, on the other hand).

17.a: A student acts as an engineer presenting a solar project in the Omani desert in three sentences, using mirror, natural gas and solar power; the class asks one question.
Pairs 'bat' sentences about an idea such as solar buses in Muscat: One advantage is … / However, a disadvantage is …; the pair that keeps going longest wins.

18.a: Teams turn rude requests (Give me the tickets!) into polite ones with would about visiting an Omani fort or museum (We would like to request …); the class claps for the politest.
The teacher names a reader (a friend, the Ministry, a hotel in Salalah); students raise a hand high or low to show formality and say a fitting greeting and closing.
Each student writes a catchy formal subject line for an email requesting a visit to an Omani place, such as a fort or a solar plant; the class votes for the best three.

19.a: Teams give a 30-second teaser of their invention using presentation language; the invention must help a place in Oman, such as a solar fan for souq stalls.
A student mimes using the team's invention and the class guesses; the inventor answers with presentation language and says how it supports Oman Vision 2040.

20.a: Teams add suffixes to words (renew – renewable, power – powerful, environment – environmental); a bonus point for a correct sentence about Oman using the new word.

21.a: A student plays a citizen of ancient Majan, the old civilisation in the land of Oman famous for copper; the class interviews him/her using ancient, culture, leader and citizen.

22.a: Students write a 'Who am I?' riddle about a civilisation or an Omani heritage place (I am made of mud bricks. I protected the town.); the class guesses.

23.a: Teams give past passive clues about an Omani landmark (It was built of stone. It was used to protect the town.); the other teams guess it.

24.a: A sentence about Omani tolerance and respect is whispered along a line; the last student rephrases it in his/her own words and the class compares it with the original.

25.a: A student gives three clues about a famous Omani person (a sailor, poet or athlete) without the name, using biography language; the class guesses who it is.
Students introduce their researched Omani person in one breath using two biography phrases (He was born in …, Later, …); the class guesses the person's job.
Volunteers each say one life event of an imagined young Omani hero and stand in chronological order; the class helps with In …, Later, … and In the end, ….

26.a: Each team gives a 20-second tour-guide teaser for its chosen site (Al Baleed, Bahla Fort, Bat tombs) to make the class want to visit; the class votes.

27.a: Groups freeze as an exhibit in a museum of Omani heritage; a 'guide' describes it with the past passive and adverbs of degree: This dhow was built by hand. It's extremely old.

0.a: Students act out a gesture and the class names its meaning using the bold words; the last gestures are Omani greetings, such as a handshake and a hand on the heart.
Pairs act a silent scene of welcoming a guest in the Omani way using body language only; the class watches and gives the scene a short title.
Teams say statements about an Omani custom or a classmate's body language; the class answers with gestures: thumbs up for True, thumbs down for False, a shrug for Not Given.
Students toss a soft ball; the thrower says a word (respect, hospitality, honest, proud) and the catcher gives another part of speech (respectful, hospitable, honesty, pride).

1.a: Pairs give one way the internet helps Oman Vision 2040 (online learning, e-services, small businesses) in one sentence; the class chooses the most useful idea.
The teacher tells a short story about a visit to the dhow yards of Sur using it, they, this and which; students shout what each reference word refers to.
Pairs write one fun sentence using today's structure about how they use the internet in Oman, e.g. planning a trip to Musandam; the class guesses which usage it shows.
Pairs act a short online chat showing good netiquette and Omani manners (greeting, respect, no rude words); the class gives a thumbs up for polite messages.

2.a: A student plays a mobile phone in the hot seat defending itself; the class asks questions and gives advantages and disadvantages, such as helping Omani families keep in touch.
A student describes a new word without saying it and the team guesses; the last word must be used in a sentence about mobile phones and life in Oman.
A student reads a short 'voice note' inviting friends to a heritage festival in Nizwa; pairs note the key words and retell it; the most accurate pair wins.
Teams write a short text message with abbreviations inviting friends to a National Day event; another team decodes it into full forms; the fastest correct team wins.

3.a: A student acts a short situation without words, e.g. a guest gently shaking the coffee cup to mean No more, thank you; the class infers the message and explains the clues.
Pairs plan a family trip to Nizwa Fort in a quick chat, taking turns to use one of today's soundbite phrases each time; the pair that uses the most phrases naturally wins.
Groups show a frozen scene of a teen talking politely to an elderly neighbour; the class guesses the scene and says one polite phrase each person could use, showing Omani respect for elders.

4.a: Groups race to invent a catchy, polite e-mail subject line inviting a foreign friend to celebrate Oman's National Day; the class votes for the best one.
The teacher reads quick e-mail habits; students stand if it follows today's rules and sit if it breaks them, then the class fixes the last one into a polite thank-you e-mail to the school cleaner.
Pairs race to write a short, correct reply to a tourist who asks by e-mail how to visit Wadi Shab, checking the greeting, paragraphs and sign-off before they read it aloud.
Groups race to say aloud a clear three-part e-mail plan (opening, main point, closing) for inviting a cousin to Muttrah Souq; the fastest clear plan wins a round of applause.

5.a: Students mime one new word from today (e.g. responsible, independent) and the class guesses it; the last mime shows a teenager helping parents prepare coffee and dates for guests.
The teacher says three short headlines; teams skim them in their heads and race to say what each full article is about, ending with a headline about young Omanis cleaning a beach.
Groups mime a short scene of teenagers helping at a family gathering in their wilaya; the class states the main idea of the scene in one clear sentence.
Teams pass a marker and write a new word from today's text on the board with its meaning; the last word must describe a good Omani citizen, e.g. helpful or honest.

6.a: Groups race to write three golden rules for good teen and parent relationships, one of them about respecting grandparents, and the class votes for the best set.
Pairs say one line from today's dialogue in different moods (angry, calm, excited) and the class guesses the mood; the final line is said calmly and respectfully, as a son speaks to his father.
Students sit in a circle and each adds one sentence using today's grammar pattern about family duties at home in Oman; anyone who freezes starts a new chain.
Students say three sentences with today's structure about their weekend with family, such as visiting grandparents in their village; the class guesses which sentence is false.

7.a: A student sits in the hot seat; classmates describe a good friend with today's adjectives (loyal, honest, kind) and he or she guesses the word, ending with the qualities of a good Omani neighbour.
Rows pass a one-sentence summary of today's listening in whispers; the last student says it aloud and the class adds one way friends in Oman help each other in hard times.
A paper ball passes around the class; whoever catches it gives one piece of advice with should or could to a new student who has moved from another wilaya and feels lonely.
Groups write a two-line rhyming poem about a true friend who helps others, like the Omani value of standing by people in need, and perform it with actions.

8.a: The teacher names items (khanjar, fast food, dishdasha, video games); students stand for 'keep our tradition' or sit for 'change is fine' and one student gives a reason with because.
A volunteer plays a grandparent; the class asks questions about life in Oman in the past (food, games, travel) and compares it with Western-style habits today.
Students pick an Omani tradition, such as Omani coffee or traditional dress, and give a 30-second talk persuading the class to keep it alive; the class claps for the most convincing.

9.a: Each student says one encouraging sentence to a classmate who is stressed before exams, using today's advice language; caring for others is a strong Omani value.
A student mimes a feeling word from today (anxious, embarrassed, confused) and the class guesses and gives advice; the last mime is a student nervous before speaking at a National Day assembly.
Teams 'buy' sentences about Omani crafts with pretend money, but only if they think the sentences are correct; the team with the most correct sentences wins.
The teacher calls parts of a letter (address, greeting, body, sign-off); students point to where it goes on an imaginary page, then one says a greeting line to a pen friend about Omani food.

10.a: A student describes a holiday in Oman with today's adjectives (exciting, relaxing, cheap) without naming the place; the class guesses, e.g. camping in the Wahiba Sands.
Two teams 'hit' tourism words back and forth (adventure, eco-tourism, cultural); the last word for each type must be a matching place in Oman, such as a fort for cultural tourism.
Groups create and perform a quick radio advert for a tourist place in Oman, such as Jebel Akhdar, using today's advert language; the class votes for the most attractive one.

11.a: Each student adds one sentence with a sequence word (first, then, after that) to a group story about a road trip from Muscat to Sur.
Pairs act out a quick phone message about meeting at the bus station before a trip to Salalah; the partner repeats the key details back to check them.
Students mingle and ask 'What are you doing this weekend?', answering with today's verb forms; each tries to find someone who plans to visit a fort, wadi or beach.
A student gives three clues about a planned trip using today's forms; the class guesses the Omani destination, for example Salalah in the khareef season.

12.a: The teacher names Omani places (Bahla Fort, Wadi Bani Khalid, Ras al Jinz); teams race to give a fitting adjective for each, and repeats are not allowed.
A student describes a place in Oman with today's phrases without saying its name; his or her team has thirty seconds to guess it.
Each student says one welcoming hotel phrase to an imaginary tourist and the next adds a new one; the chain ends by offering Omani coffee and dates.

13.a: A paper ball passes around; whoever catches it answers a tourist's question about their own wilaya, such as 'Where can I buy Omani halwa?'.
Students form two circles; 'tourists' ask and 'information officers' answer with today's phrases about Omani places, moving round every thirty seconds.
Groups create a two-line rhyming slogan recommending a place in Oman to visitors, such as a traditional souq, and perform it to the class.

14.a: Groups invent a catchy name for a one-day heritage tour of Oman (forts, souqs, falaj) and explain their choice in one sentence; the class votes.
A student holds a pretend microphone and gives one line of a tour with today's tour language ('On your left you can see...'), then passes it on; the tour is of Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque.
Groups mime a day trip (drive, swim in a wadi, picnic, clean up, go home) and the class narrates it with sequence words.

15.a: Students mime using a smart home device; the class guesses it and says how it could save water or electricity in an Omani home.
Pairs invent a smart gadget to help an Omani family, such as one that waters date palms on time, and present it in two sentences.

16.a: A student thinks of an Omani symbol (khanjar, dhow, frankincense); the class asks yes/no questions to guess it in twenty questions or fewer.
The teacher says a verb; the class claps and calls out its past participle, then a volunteer makes a passive sentence about Oman, e.g. 'Frankincense is collected in Dhofar.'
Students say passive sentences about an Omani item without naming it ('It is made of silver and worn on special days'); the class guesses (a khanjar).

17.a: The teacher names inventions; students show thumbs up or down and say 'The best/worst thing about it is...', ending with plastic bags on Oman's beaches.
The teacher says a root word and teams race to say another form of it; the last words are nation, tradition and honest (national, traditional, honesty).

18.a: Pairs imagine a virtual reality tour of an Omani site, like a dhow yard in Sur, and describe in two sentences what visitors can see and do there.
Each student turns a direct tourist question into an indirect one ('Could you tell me where Nizwa Souq is?') and the next student answers it politely.

19.a: The teacher reads quick online offers; students stand for a fair deal or sit for a suspicious one, then the class says why honesty in trade, as in Omani souqs, matters.
Pairs act out a polite complaint and reply about an online order of Omani dates that arrived late, using today's language; then they swap roles.

0.a: Groups race to make a short slogan with two core words (brand, persuade, bargaining) to sell Omani handicrafts; the class votes for the most persuasive.
The teacher says a comparing phrase; students row with their arms for the dhow or make a horn sound for the tanker, and one says why dhows are part of Oman's heritage.
Groups build a short story of an Omani merchant sailing old trade routes, each student adding a sentence with one of today's words (merchants, routes, exported).

1.a: Groups invent a brand name and a simple logo idea for an Omani product, such as frankincense perfume or halwa, and present it in one sentence.
Students say a past passive sentence about something in Oman without naming it ('It was built to protect the town'); the class guesses (a fort).
A student mimes a hospitality action (coffee is poured, dates are served) and the class describes it with a past simple passive sentence.
Groups tell the history of an invented Omani brand, taking turns with past simple and past simple passive sentences; the smoothest story wins.

2.a: A volunteer acts as a shopaholic; classmates ask questions and give advice about wise spending and supporting local Omani markets.
The teacher names items; students move left for 'need' and right for 'want', and one explains why; the round ends with saving money to help others.
The teacher says a noun; students clap once for make and twice for do, then a volunteer says a sentence such as 'Young people can make a difference in Oman.'

3.a: The teacher reads a sentence; students point left for a mall or right for a souq, ending with 'You can bargain with friendly sellers' for Muttrah Souq.
Students act as sellers in a traditional Omani souq, calling out their goods (dates, frankincense, silver) and the class guesses what each one sells.
The teacher asks questions like 'Would you rather shop in Nizwa Souq or a big mall?'; students answer with today's preference phrases and a reason.

4.a: Groups make a frozen picture of a TV advert telling people to keep Oman's beaches clean; the class guesses their slogan.
Teams bid to describe an Omani product like halwa with the best advertising adjective (fresh, rich, traditional); the most persuasive bid wins.
Pairs perform a 20-second advert for an Omani product, once as hard-sell and once as soft-sell; the class decides which works better.

5.a: The teacher draws two circles; students call out things for Egypt, Oman or both (desert, river, mountains, hospitality, old history) to compare the two Arab countries.
Groups create a fully honest two-line advert for an Omani product, showing honesty as an Omani value, and the class checks it is not misleading.

6.a: Students mime core words (apprehensive, confident, independent) and the class guesses; then each says one way an Omani graduate can serve the country.
Pairs think of one tip for a new student at Sultan Qaboos University, share it with another pair and the class picks the most helpful tip.
A volunteer plays a nervous first-year student; classmates use today's words (apprehensive, homesick) to ask questions and encourage him or her, showing care for others.
The teacher names a text (a road sign, a novel, a news report about National Day); students mime the speed (slow walk or fast run) and name the reading type.

7.a: Pairs take turns: one says a university problem and the partner offers help, like Abdullah helping Faisal; helping a newcomer is an Omani value.
Students hear two past events and jump left for the one that had happened first, then say a past perfect sentence, e.g. about preparing for National Day.
Groups build a story about a student's first week in Muscat, each adding a sentence that uses the past perfect.

8.a: Students say one thing they would pack to share Omani culture while studying abroad (dates, coffee, a photo of the flag) and give a reason.
The teacher says sentences with a made-up word ('We drank hot zibble with dates'); students guess the real meaning from context (coffee).
The teacher says four words; students find the odd one and name the field the others belong to; the last set is khanjar, dhow, frankincense, laptop.

9.a: Pairs act out a lost new student and an SQU Rover who helps; the class says why volunteering to help others makes Oman stronger.
A student whispers a message about meeting at a heritage village; the listener uses today's clarification phrases to check every detail before passing it on.
Students move to the 'true' or 'false' side of the room for statements about Oman (Muscat is the capital of Oman) and correct any false one.

10.a: The teacher reads a sentence welcoming a new teacher to Oman; students jump for full stops, wave for commas and stretch up for capital letters.
A student says a sentence about his or her wilaya; the partner notes only key words and repeats the full idea from the notes.
The teacher reads expressions; students bow for formal and wave for informal, then one says a formal welcome to a guest in the Omani way.

11.a: Pairs role-play telling a French tourist three things to see in Oman, comparing them with places in France from today's reading.
A student plays an Omani explorer just back from Antarctica; classmates ask questions about the trip and how young Omanis can protect nature at home.

12.a: Each student greets a 'tourist' with a welcoming sentence using one core word (stunning, scenery, variety) and offers Omani coffee.
A student says a tourist's opinion ('The view from the top was amazing') and the class guesses the Omani place, such as Jebel Shams.
Students mime explore, trek and proud; the class guesses and makes a sentence with the word about Wadi Ghul, known as Oman's Grand Canyon.

13.a: A student mimes a tourism job (chef, tour guide, cabin crew); the class guesses and names one quality needed to welcome visitors to Oman.
Each student builds on the last result: 'If I become a tour guide, I will show visitors Nizwa Fort.' 'If I show them Nizwa Fort, they will...'

14.a: The teacher gives three clues about a country and teams scan their memory to guess it; the final clues describe Oman.
A paper ball passes; when the teacher says 'boom', the holder makes a sentence about tourism in Oman with one of today's words (draw, flock, architecture).

15.a: Pairs give a one-sentence pitch on why they would be a great Omani tour guide or chef; the class votes for the best pitch.
Groups create a three-dish menu of Omani food (shuwa, harees, halwa) for a hotel and present it with today's words.
Pairs perform a funny, over-the-top complaint at a hotel and a polite, calm reply in the spirit of Omani hospitality; the class votes for the best reply.

16.a: A student mimes eating an Omani dish (shuwa, mashuai, halwa) and gives a review; the class guesses the dish.
Each student adds a sentence with a linking word to a story about a family dinner during Eid.
The teacher starts a story about a tourist trying Omani halwa for the first time; groups invent a funny ending and share it.

17.a: The teacher says features of Canada or Oman; students shiver for Canada or fan their faces for Oman, then one compares them in a sentence.
A student describes an Omani dish's taste with adjectives; the class guesses which dish it is.

18.a: Students mime core words (road rage, congestion, ambitious) and the class guesses; the last word links to ambitious plans in Oman Vision 2040.
The teacher reads statements about Oman; students stand for true, sit for false and shrug for not given, then fix a false one.

19.a: Groups mime a traffic jam; the class describes the feelings with today's words, then suggests one polite way drivers can show respect on Oman's roads.
Students mingle asking 'Have you ever visited Sur?' or 'How long have you been learning English?' and find someone for each question.

20.a: The teacher describes driver behaviours; students show thumbs up or down and give a reason, thanking the ROP for keeping Oman's roads safe.
The teacher says trend phrases (rise sharply, fall slightly, remain steady); students show them with their arms, then make a sentence about trees planted at school.

21.a: A student gives an unclear description of an airport job; classmates ask 'What do you mean by...?' until they guess the job.

22.a: Students line up as a train; each adds a clause with a conjunction about the benefits of trains for Oman, then joins the train.
Groups create a rail safety slogan using because or so and share it, explaining how it keeps people in Oman safe.

23.a: The teacher says a feature (windmills, forts, coffee, monarchy); students call out Spain, Oman or both and explain.

0.a: The teacher draws the Oman flag on the board and gives instructions (look, listen, point, draw); pupils do them, e.g. point to the red, then wave goodbye.

1.a: Pupils form a train; each says 'My name's... I'm seven' and greets the next pupil with a smile and 'Welcome!', like Omani hospitality.

2.a: The teacher draws dates on the board; the class counts aloud to ten and says the colour; dates are a gift for guests in Oman.

3.a: A pupil mimes playing with a toy; the class asks 'What's this?' and answers 'It's a car!'; the last mime is a toy dhow.

4.a: Pupils form a train and chug around; when the teacher says an ai word they stop and say /eɪ/, and the train 'stops' at a station called Sohar.

5.a: Pupils move around; when the teacher shows a toy, they freeze and say its name; at the end they share a toy and say 'Thank you'.

6.a: Pupils sit in rows, row their arms and chant oa words (boat, coat, goat, road, soap); the teacher says 'Our boat is a dhow from Sur!'

7.a: The teacher names outdoor toys and pupils act playing; then, on 'Clean up!', pupils pick up pretend rubbish and say 'Keep our park clean!'

8.a: Pupils say /aɪ/ and mime eating a pie; then the teacher asks 'Who likes Omani halwa?' and pupils raise hands saying 'I do!'

9.a: The teacher draws slowly; pupils ask 'Is it a ...?' to guess the toy; the last drawing is a kite flying over an Omani beach.

10.a: Pupils make a snake line and hiss through the class saying a-e words (snake, lake, cake); the snake stops at the lake and says 'Keep our wadis clean!'

11.a: Pupils point to and name things you can do in the museum and mime them (ride a bike, play with puppets), saying 'I love Oman's museums!'

12.a: Pupils sing 'Can I play, please? Yes, of course!' to a known tune with clapping, sharing toys like families in Oman share.

13.a: The teacher describes a toy by colour and size; pupils guess 'Is it a ...?'; the last toy is a camel toy.

14.a: The teacher draws a lake line on the floor; pupils jump into the 'lake' when they hear an a-e word, then help a friend jump in.
The teacher reads a sentence in a funny voice (big, small, happy); pupils echo; the last sentence is 'We are happy in Oman!'
Pupils mime opening a present; the class guesses 'It's a kite!' and pupils say 'Thank you', showing gratitude.

15.a: Pupils pack their bags saying 'These are my books' and 'This is my pen', respecting school property.

16.a: The teacher says or words and pupils act (storm: shake, torch: shine); then they say 'Our flag is red, white and green.'

17.a: Pupils walk around; the teacher holds up one or more objects and pupils freeze and say 'This is a pen' or 'These are pens'.

18.a: Pupils swing arms and sing ng words (ring, sing, bang, long); the last line is 'We sing for Oman!'

19.a: The teacher gives instructions like 'Put your pencil on the desk'; then asks 'Where's the Oman flag?' and pupils answer 'It's on the wall'.

20.a: Pupils mime cook, look, book; the teacher says 'Look! A cook makes Omani bread', and pupils ask 'Why?' and guess the answer.

21.a: Pupils point to an object and say 'It's on the desk. It's green'; one says 'Green like the palm trees in Oman'.

22.a: Pupils walk slowly like on the moon for long oo words and tip-toe for short oo; the teacher says 'Look at the moon over the desert'.

23.a: Pupils act walking to places (library, playground) and say 'This is our library'; they promise to keep our school clean.

24.a: Pupils dance; when the teacher says a word they freeze in the action for its sound; the final word is boat, for an Omani dhow.

25.a: The teacher asks to borrow things; pupils only give if 'please' is used, then say 'Thank you', showing Omani good manners.

26.a: The teacher says ch-ai-n, sp-or-t, br-oo-m sound by sound; the class blends the word and jumps once. Last word: f-or-t, like Nizwa Fort, and pupils say 'Our fort!' proudly.

27.a: The teacher says This is my bag / These are my pens; pupils point to one or many things. Then pupils help tidy the classroom together, saying These are our books, because a clean Oman starts in class.

28.a: The teacher says three words; pupils stand up when they hear the odd sound out. Last set uses dates, flag, fort words, and pupils clap for Oman's flag colours: red, white, green.

29.a: Pupils mime brushing their teeth while chanting oo and or words from 'My tooth'. They end by saying Thank you to a family member, as polite Omani children do.
Small groups freeze in a picture from 'My tooth'; the class guesses which part it is. Groups end by smiling and helping each other up, showing kindness like good Omani friends.

30.a: The teacher calls Very big! or Very small!; pupils stretch tall or crouch down. Last call: Very big mountain like Jebel Shams! and everyone stretches high with arms up.

31.a: Pupils pretend to walk in a busy souq: the teacher says I can see dates, I can smell coffee, I can hear people; pupils point to eyes, nose or ears and repeat.

32.a: The class chants I've got two arms, I've got two legs with actions, then freezes like a statue. Last line: I've got two hands to help my friends, and pupils shake hands.

33.a: The teacher whispers ou words (cloud, mouth, count); pupils do the ou action and shout the word. They end by counting together to ten in English and saying We all love Oman.

34.a: One pupil is Gymbot and says I've got a white head; the class copies a robot exercise. Gymbot ends with a move to show we keep healthy and strong for Oman.

35.a: The teacher hides a paper coin; pupils say oi words (coin, oil, soil) while guessing where it is. The finder says Can I have some dates? and the class shares a pretend plate, like Omani hospitality.

36.a: The class plays Simon says with move, bend, stretch, touch, stamp, clap. Last command: Clap for Oman! and everyone claps and waves a pretend flag.

37.a: The teacher gives a clue with ue words: It is blue and big, near the beach. Pupils guess the sea and mime swimming, then say Give me your rubbish to keep Oman's beaches clean.

38.a: The class sings the unit song and does the moves; when the music stops, the teacher says a body part and pupils touch it. Final freeze: pupils stand tall like guards at a fort.

39.a: Pupils draw a robot in the air as the teacher says I've got a red head, green arms. The last robot is red, white and green like the Omani flag, and pupils say its colours.

40.a: The teacher says i-e words (kite, bike, slide, dive, drive); pupils mime each one. Last word: kite, and pupils pretend to fly kites on a beach in Oman, keeping the beach clean.

41.a: Pupils dance freely; when the teacher calls a move (Stamp your feet! Bend your arms!) they do it and freeze. The final move is a polite wave to welcome a guest, Omani style.

42.a: The class marches like a National Day parade, waving pretend flags and saying red, white, green. Pupils name one thing they wear on National Day, like a kumma or a colourful dress.

43.a: Four corners show ou, oi, ue and i-e. The teacher says a word and pupils walk to the right corner. Last word: coin, and pupils say We save coins to help people in need.

44.a: Groups get big letter cards and stand in order to spell a Unit 3 word, like cloud or coin. The winning group says a fort word too: f-or-t, and the class cheers.

45.a: Pairs face each other; one does a cool pose and the other says What a cool robot! / What a nice smile! and copies it, then says Thank you. Kind words are part of good Omani manners.

46.a: One pupil mimes a body word (arms, feet, head); the class writes it in the air and says it. The last mime is shaking hands to welcome a friend, as people do in Oman.

47.a: The teacher says a sentence from the story; pupils hop forward if it comes early and back if it comes late. They end by saying a kind compliment to the class, as polite Omani children do.

48.a: Pupils mime digging while the teacher tells parts of 'The big dig'. They pretend to find an old pot and say Wow! like finding treasure from Oman's long history.
The teacher reads a line from 'The big dig' in a funny voice; pupils echo it. The last line is We all work together, and pupils link arms like a team helping in the wilaya.
Pupils sit and pedal pretend bikes while the teacher retells 'My bike'. When they hear blue or glue they stand up. They end by riding past a pretend wadi and waving to friends.

49.a: Teams pass a ball; each child says a body or movement word before passing. The last child says a kind action, such as help, and the team cheers for helping others in Oman.

50.a: Two volunteers act as robots and describe themselves: I've got blue arms. The class claps and copies one move. The robots end by saying I help keep my school clean.

51.a: Pupils hold up fingers and say Who's this? It's my grandpa / grandma / uncle. They end by showing a pretend cup and saying In Oman, we serve coffee to our family.

52.a: The class sings ee words to a simple tune (sheep, feet, sleep, sweet) and does the actions. The last line is Sweet, sweet dates from Oman! and pupils pretend to share dates with a friend.

53.a: Pupils pass a soft ball like Lily's family game; the catcher says He's got the ball or She's got the ball. They end by saying I love my family, a strong value in Oman.

54.a: The teacher says er words; pupils mime: herd (walk like goats), perfume (spray and smell), person (wave). Last: smell pretend Omani frankincense and say Come and see!

55.a: The teacher describes a hidden person: She's got brown eyes and black hair. Pupils guess who. Last description is a friendly Omani grandpa with a white kumma, and pupils wave.

56.a: The teacher says ar words; pupils mime: star (twinkle hands), shark (swim), farm (dig), park (run). Last: star, and pupils say What do you see? I see stars over the Omani desert.

57.a: Groups stand like a family tree (grandpa at top, children below) and say who they are. They end by bowing politely to their 'grandparents', showing respect as Omani families do.

58.a: One pupil describes a family member: He's got short hair and brown eyes. The class guesses grandpa, uncle or brother. The pupil ends by saying one way they help that person at home.

59.a: The teacher says o-e words (home, rose, rope, stone, nose); pupils mime them. Last word: home, and pupils make a roof with their arms and say Oman is my home.

60.a: One pupil gives monster orders: Show three eyes! Show two noses! The class makes funny faces with fingers. The last order is Show a big smile, because Omanis welcome visitors with smiles.

61.a: The class mimes a birthday: blow candles, give a present, say Happy birthday! Pupils then offer a pretend plate of dates and halwa to a guest, like Omani hospitality.

62.a: The teacher says a word; pupils hop left for ee, right for ar, forward for er, back for o-e. Last word: farm, and pupils mime picking dates on an Omani farm.

63.a: Pupils make a train; the driver says This is my friend. His name's ... and the friend joins the train saying Nice to meet you! They end with a hand on the heart, an Omani greeting.

64.a: The teacher says a word: if it has ee, pupils baa like sheep; if ar, they swim like sharks. Last word: dark, and pupils say Good night, Oman! with a sleeping action.

65.a: The teacher holds up a word card; pupils make the action for its sound (ee, er, ar, o-e). Last card: garden, and pupils mime watering plants to keep Oman green.

66.a: Groups pose for a pretend family photo and say This is my mum, my uncle, my sister. Then they say one thing they do with family on Eid, like visiting grandma.

67.a: Pupils walk like goats while the teacher retells 'The goat herd'. When they hear herd, feet, farm or nose they stop and point. They end by saying goats live in Oman's mountains.
Pairs read a page from 'The goat herd' in funny voices (big goat, small goat). They end by saying Thank you to their partner, a polite habit Omani children practise.
The teacher hides a paper shark; pupils guess Is it under the desk? using story words. The finder says Sharks swim in the sea near Oman's beaches, and the class mimes swimming.

68.a: The class makes up a short chant: Mum and Dad, sister and brother, we help each other! with actions. They end with Love your family, love Oman! and clap.

69.a: Pupils draw a monster in the air while one child says There is one head, there are four legs. The last monster wears a kumma, and pupils laugh and say There is a kumma!

70.a: The class becomes a town: some pupils are the school, hospital, shops. Others walk and say There is a ... They end by naming a good place in their own wilaya, like a fort or a park.

71.a: Pupils stand in a circle and each says one English word they love from this semester, then passes a paper star. The last child says Oman, and everyone claps for a great semester.

0.a: One pupil is the teacher and gives classroom commands: Put up your hand! Pay attention! The class obeys. The last command is Pick up the rubbish!, because we keep our school and Oman clean.

1.a: Pupils sit in a circle and spell an Omani name or place letter by letter, one letter each: S-O-H-A-R, M-U-S-C-A-T. The class shouts the word at the end and claps.

2.a: Pupils point and say This is / That is / These are / Those are about classroom things, counting 11 to 20. The last item is a picture of the Omani flag: That is our flag! and pupils salute.

3.a: The teacher calls a routine (get up, pray, have breakfast, go to bed); pupils mime it quickly and say I ... or We don't .... They end with We help our family at home, a good Omani value.

4.a: The teacher calls a colour from the story; pupils touch something in that colour and freeze like Atomic. The last call is red, white and green, and pupils point to the Omani flag colours.

5.a: The teacher says a time of day; pupils mime a routine for it (morning: wash, night: sleep). They then ask a partner When do you visit your grandparents? and answer In the evening.

6.a: The teacher mimes a routine and holds up fingers for the time; pupils say He gets up in the morning. The last mime is praying at noon, a part of daily life in Oman.

7.a: Pupils describe a pretend breakfast plate with words like porridge, tea, toast; the class guesses the country. The last plate is khubz rakhal and tea, and pupils say It's Oman!

8.a: Two pupils make a clock with their arms; the class says the time (half past, quarter to). Last time: What time do we visit the souq? and pupils answer with a time they choose.

9.a: The teacher says wh and ph words; pupils swim like whales for wh and wave like dolphins for ph. They end by saying Dolphins swim near the Omani coast, and we keep the sea clean.

10.a: The teacher says a sentence like We pray in the morning or We go to bed at noon; pupils stand for true and sit for false. The last one is We help our neighbours, and everyone stands.

11.a: One pupil mimes something; the class guesses morning, afternoon, evening or night. The last mime is drinking Omani coffee with dates in the afternoon with guests.

12.a: Pupils stand in a line as board squares; a child rolls a pretend dice and the class gives instructions: Go forward two spaces! The final square says Help a friend! and pupils high-five.

13.a: Pupils walk like robots and say Robot routines: I get up at seven. When the teacher says Stop!, they freeze and say one good habit, like I keep my classroom clean.

14.a: The teacher says a clothes word; pupils point to it on a friend: You're wearing a shirt. The last words are dishdasha and hijab, and pupils say We're wearing Omani clothes!
Volunteers walk like models; the class describes them: She's wearing a hijab. They're wearing trainers. The last model wears a pretend kumma for National Day, and everyone claps.

15.a: Groups freeze as characters from 'The school show'; the class guesses who and says what they are wearing. The last group shows children sharing clothes, and the teacher says sharing is kind.
The teacher says actions (leave the tap on, reuse a bag); pupils thumbs up for not wasteful, thumbs down for wasteful. They end with We save water in Oman because water is precious.

16.a: The teacher puts possessions on a table (keys, glasses, phone), then hides one; groups guess What's missing? using Our / Their. The last thing hidden is a small Omani flag.
Pupils pass a possession around; the teacher stops it and asks Whose is it? Pupils say It's our / their / your book. They end with This is our country, Oman! and clap.

17.a: The teacher describes two pupils: They're wearing white shirts. Their shoes are black. The class guesses who. The last pair are 'wearing' pretend kummas, and pupils say the word.

18.a: Pupils mime Eid things one by one: giving Eidiya, eating sweets, opening presents, wearing new clothes. The class guesses and says Eid Mubarak! to each other with a smile.
Groups hold up their special-day posters and say one sentence: They're wearing .... The class gives a cheer for each one and names one special day in Oman they like.

19.a: The teacher holds up a classroom object and pupils guess How much is it? It's ... rials. The last thing is a pretend bag of Omani dates, and pupils say It's sweet and cheap!

20.a: The teacher says words; pupils touch their ear for ear words (hear, beard) and draw a frame for ure words (picture). The last word is picture, and pupils draw a fort picture in the air.

21.a: The teacher says a sentence; pupils jump left for They're and right for Their. The last sentence is Their dishdashas are white, and pupils point to something white.
Pairs stand up and introduce each other: I'm Salim. He's my friend. We're wearing ... They end by saying one good thing about their friend, because respect is an Omani value.

22.a: The teacher says sentences about the room; pupils make a tick with their arm or a cross with their arms. The last one: The Omani flag is red, white and green, and they all tick.

23.a: The teacher calls You're wearing something white!; pupils wearing it stand and freeze. The last call is red, white and green, the colours of the Omani flag, and everyone waves.

24.a: One pupil mimes putting on clothes (a coat, a hijab, trainers); the class guesses She's wearing .... The last mime is wearing a kumma for National Day, and pupils say the word.

25.a: The class chants a quick rhyme with actions: Our school, your bag, their caps, their house! The last line is Our flag, our Oman! and pupils wave pretend flags.

26.a: Pupils count ten, twenty ... one hundred, clapping on each number. The last number: one hundred, and pupils say We love Oman one hundred times! with a big cheer.

27.a: Groups guess how long things are in centimetres (a pencil, a desk) and the teacher checks. The last thing is a picture of a khanjar, and pupils say It is long and silver.

28.a: One pupil mimes an activity (ride a bike, do karate); the class says He plays ... / She doesn't .... The last mime is playing football on the beach, which many children in Oman enjoy.
Pupils walk and ask Do you ride a bike? Do you play tennis? They report: Ali plays tennis. The last question is Do you help at home? and pupils say who helps, a good Omani habit.

29.a: The teacher says a time (9, 10, 11 o'clock); pupils freeze as Fatma at that time. They end by sitting under a pretend tree for a rest and say We take care of trees in Oman.

30.a: Seven pupils hold day cards and others put them in order. Friday and Saturday step forward and say We are the weekend in Oman! and everyone cheers.
The teacher says Does he visit grandma on Fridays? Pupils answer Yes, he does / No, he doesn't. They end by telling a partner one thing they do with family at the weekend.

31.a: A pupil thinks of a day for an activity; the class asks Does he roller-skate on Wednesdays? until they guess. The last activity is visiting a fort on Saturdays.

32.a: Two teams race in place: one team rides pretend camels, the other rows pretend dhows, saying I like camel racing because .... Both teams finish together and clap for Omani heritage.

33.a: The teacher reads actions; pupils stand for always, crouch for often, sit for never. The last action is I always say Salaam to my neighbours, and everyone stands.

34.a: One pupil is the magic e with a pretend wand; they touch a word card (cub, kit, tub) and the class says the new word (cube, kite, tube). The last word is kite, flying over a beach in Oman.

35.a: The teacher throws a soft ball with a question: Does Ahmed swim on Fridays? The catcher answers Yes, he does / No, he doesn't. The last question is about helping clean the beach.
Pupils mime what a family member always or often does on Saturday; the partner guesses: She always cooks lunch. They end by saying one thing their family does to welcome guests.

36.a: The teacher says sentences about a picture; pupils run to the Yes or No side of the class. The last one: On Fridays, many families in Oman visit their grandparents. Yes!

37.a: One pupil mimes an activity and holds up a day card; the class asks Does he play tennis on Mondays? Yes, he does. The last mime is visiting grandparents on Fridays, an Omani family habit.

38.a: Pupils mime fun at the park while the teacher retells the story; when Badriya helps, pupils help a partner stand up. They end by saying We help our friends, like good Omanis.

39.a: One pupil mimes a job; the class guesses and says I want to be a / an .... The last mime is a fisherman on a dhow, an old job in Oman, and pupils say He's a fisherman.

40.a: Pupils walk in a line and each says I want to be a ... to help Oman, with an action. The class claps and the teacher reminds them that Oman needs many jobs for Vision 2040.

41.a: The class makes a train line and moves around; the teacher calls bus, boat, car, motorbike and pupils change actions. The last stop: My father goes to work by car on Oman's roads, and they wave.

42.a: A pupil whispers a job and transport to the teacher; the class asks Is she a nurse? Does she go by bus? The last secret person is a fisherman who goes to work by boat from an Omani beach.

43.a: The class plays bus driver and students: the driver calls Stop! and students get on politely, saying Thank you. They end by saying We sit nicely and keep our school bus clean.

44.a: Teams whisper a phone message down the line: Hello, it's Maha. Come to Muttrah Souq at four! The last pupil says it aloud; the team with the right message wins.

45.a: The teacher says ea words; pupils stretch arms wide for long ea (beach, read) and clap once for short ea (bread, weather). Last word: beach, and pupils say Let's keep our beaches clean!

46.a: One pupil mimes a job and a transport together (a pilot by plane, a chef by bus); the class says She's a chef. She goes to work by bus. The last mime is a doctor helping people in Oman.

47.a: Pupils stand in a circle and each says I want to be a ... with an action. The teacher ends by saying All these jobs help build Oman, and the class gives one big clap.

48.a: Each pupil mimes the job they want and a transport; the class says She wants to be a pilot. She goes by plane. The last one is a fisherman going by dhow, and pupils mime rowing.

49.a: A pupil describes clothes for a job: I'm wearing a white coat; the class guesses doctor. The last one wears school clothes, and pupils say Learning helps us build Oman.

50.a: The teacher says a season; pupils mime the weather (shiver for winter, fan face for summer). They end by saying In Oman summer is very hot and winter is nice for camping in the desert.

51.a: The class chants the twelve months with three claps after each season. Then pupils say the month of their birthday and the teacher says We celebrate Omani National Day every year too.

0.a: Pupils toss a soft ball; the catcher says I'm (name), I'm nine and I'm from Oman / Egypt / India. The last catcher says I'm Omani and I'm proud of it!, and the class claps.

1.a: One pupil mimes a hobby (canoeing, reading); the class guesses and says I like / I don't like it. The last mime is canoeing in a wadi, and pupils name a wadi in Oman they know.

2.a: One pupil sits on the hot seat; classmates give clues about a subject or school place (We use a ball. We run.). The pupil guesses PE. The last clue is about Social Studies: We learn about Oman.

3.a: One pupil is a magnet and calls a school word; pupils holding that pretend object 'stick' to the magnet. The last call is We all stick together, like Omanis helping each other.

4.a: Pupils make a human clock and ask When do you have Maths? I have Maths at quarter past nine. The last question is When do you sing the national anthem? and they answer In the morning.

5.a: The teacher says actions; pupils stand on a line from always to never. The last one: I always throw rubbish in the bin to keep Oman clean, and pupils run to always.

6.a: Pairs choose one unusual school they would visit and say why in one sentence. They then imagine a school in a fort or by a wadi in Oman, and the class votes for the most fun idea.

7.a: Pupils draw a quick weekend diary with two free times, then find a friend with the same free time: Let's meet at half past four! They choose a fun place in Oman, like a park or the beach.

8.a: The teacher reads feeling words from Maryam's diary; pupils freeze as statues showing nervous, happy or excited. The last feeling is proud, when we see the Omani flag at school.

9.a: Pupils walk and ask What do you do after school? Do you play football? They find a friend for each activity. The last question is Do you help your family? and pupils share one way.

10.a: Teams race to say long i words with ie, igh, i-e or y; each word adds a 'kite' to the board. Last words: bye and my, and pupils say Bye! My country is Oman!

11.a: Teams run to stand in alphabetical order holding subject names (Art, English, Maths, Science). They then ask How often do we study Social Studies? and say We learn about Oman twice a week.
Pairs make a quick arrangement: Let's meet at the fort at four o'clock. That's a good idea! They choose a well-known place in their wilaya and say why they like it.

12.a: Groups add one sentence each to describe an imaginary picture of a family day at the beach in Oman. The group with the funniest sentence wins a big clap.

13.a: Pairs act as tour guides and show a visitor around the school: This is the science lab. This is the garden. They end with Welcome to our school! and offer pretend dates, as in Omani hospitality.

14.a: The teacher calls food words; pupils go left for sweet and right for savoury. The last items are dates and halwa, and pupils say They're sweet, Omani favourites!

15.a: Groups brainstorm one fun thing to do with an old shed, using food words: a café with sandwiches and juice. The best idea includes serving coffee and dates to guests, Omani style.
The teacher says silly sentences like Bo! There are a lot of shoes in the cake. Pupils correct them quickly. The last one: Omani coffee is pink! and pupils correct the colour with a laugh.

16.a: The teacher describes a hidden basket: There are a few sandwiches. There is a little juice. Pupils guess the items. The last item is a lot of dates, shared like Omani hospitality.

17.a: Teams take turns saying a container phrase (a can of lemonade, a bowl of soup) without repeating. The last phrase is a pot of Omani coffee, and both teams cheer.
One pupil imagines a picnic basket; the class asks Is there any juice? Are there any dates? The pupil answers. They end by saying In Oman we always share food with our guests.

18.a: Pupils stand along a line to show how much they want to try each dish (sushi, fondue, bubble tea). Then they say which Omani dish a visitor must try, like shuwa or harees.
Groups stand by their food posters; others visit and ask What's it called? What's in it? Each group answers in one sentence about their Omani dish and invites them to taste it.

19.a: The class plays a chain game: I went to the souq and bought a bag of dates. The next pupil repeats and adds an item. Pupils say That's ... rials at the end and thank the shopkeeper.

20.a: The teacher reads recipe instructions (cut, mix, pour, cook); pupils mime them like chefs. The last step is serve the food to your family, and pupils say Enjoy your meal!

21.a: Groups agree a quick menu for three friends with different tastes, saying He likes ... She doesn't like .... They add one Omani dish everyone can share, like rice and fish.
Groups get recipe steps for a cup of Omani coffee and stand in order, saying First, then, after that, last. The class checks and gives a clap for each good order.

22.a: The teacher says long o words; pupils row for oa (boat), shiver for ow (snow), point for o-e (bone). The last word is boat, and pupils say Dhows are traditional Omani boats.

23.a: Pairs make one quick food riddle: It's sweet and brown. It grows on palm trees. The class guesses dates. Pupils then share one more Omani food riddle with the class.
The teacher says a sentence with a mistake: There are some milk. Pupils stand and correct it: There is some milk. The last sentence is about Omani coffee and dates for guests.

24.a: The teacher says four words (dates, coffee, halwa, car); pupils stand up, say which one is different and why (They are food, a car is not). The last set is Omani heritage: khanjar, dhow, kumma, pizza.

25.a: Groups pass a whispered sentence about a new shop in Muttrah Souq along their line; the last pupil says it aloud and the class checks if the news travelled correctly, like Hamzah's news.

26.a: Pairs describe an Omani object by size and shape (It's rectangular and red, white and green. It's a flag! It's small and round. It's a date!) and their partner guesses it.

27.a: Groups stand as a souq shelf: one pupil at the top, one in the middle, one at the bottom, each holding a pretend item (dates, halwa, frankincense); the class says 'The halwa is above the dates.'

28.a: A pupil mimes a landscape (a high mountain, a wide beach, a deep wadi); the class guesses with adjective + noun, then the pupil says one place in Oman they want to visit.

29.a: The teacher calls a rubbish item (a plastic bottle, an old box, a can); pupils mime a way to reuse it, then the class says together: 'We keep our wadis and beaches clean!'

30.a: Pairs race to make comparatives about Omani things (A camel is taller than a goat. The desert is hotter than the mountains.); the fastest pairs read one sentence to the class.

31.a: Groups race to say a superlative sentence about Oman (Jebel Shams is the highest mountain in Oman) and one about the class (Saif is the tallest); the class claps for correct -est forms.

32.a: A pupil gives a clue about a nature reserve (It has islands and turtles.) and the class shouts its name; then each row says one rule for protecting nature in Oman.
Each group makes a short slogan with a superlative for its reserve (Visit the most beautiful islands in Oman!) and chants it with claps; the class chooses the catchiest slogan.

33.a: The teacher draws a quick map with a fort, a souq and a beach; teams direct a volunteer's finger (turn left, go straight ahead) to one place, then say 'Welcome to Oman!'

34.a: Groups make a frozen picture of a scene from Wadi rescue!; the class guesses the scene, then says one wadi safety rule (Don't swim in a wadi when it is raining).

35.a: A pupil says three key words about a favourite place in Oman (sand, camels, hot) and the class guesses it (the desert!); the winner gives the next three key words.
The teacher says words (muscat, river, nizwa, mountain, salalah, sur); pupils stand up if the word needs a capital letter and write the capital letter in the air.

36.a: The class chants 'Eight neighbours weigh eight dates', clapping on each /eɪ/ sound; groups add actions, then say one way we help our neighbours in Oman.

37.a: A pupil pretends to be an animal from Oman (a camel, an Arabian oryx, a turtle) and gives clues (I'm bigger than a goat. I live in the desert.); the class guesses the animal.

38.a: Pairs quickly draw a beach with a dhow and three other things, then find four differences between their pictures (In my picture the dhow is big, but in yours it's small).

39.a: Two pupils mime rowing boats like old Omani fishermen; the class commentates with comparatives (Qais is quicker! Yasir is wetter! Now he's slower!) until the finish line.

40.a: Pupils pass a ball; the catcher says a job, where the person works and how they help Oman (A nurse works in a hospital. She helps sick people.), then passes it on.

41.a: A pupil sits in the hot seat as Alesha; classmates ask about her job and family, then the class says one way we respect older people in our family.

42.a: The teacher says 'Freeze! You're at the souq'; a group freezes in a scene (buying dates, pouring coffee); the class describes them (He's buying dates. She's wearing a red scarf.).

43.a: Groups make two must/mustn't rules for a beach in Oman (We must put litter in the bin. We mustn't drop litter on the sand.) and perform them as a short rap with a beat.

44.a: A pupil thinks of an unusual job in Oman (falconer, dhow builder, potter); the class asks yes/no questions (Do you work outside? Do you work with animals?) to guess it.

45.a: Pupils mime an emergency worker (a firefighter, a police officer, a paramedic); the class says who they are and where they work, then says 'Thank you for keeping Oman safe!'

46.a: The four corners are interesting, boring, dangerous and exciting; the teacher says a job (fisherman, pilot, farmer); pupils walk to a corner and say why they chose it.

47.a: Pupils line up in groups by dream job and each says 'I want to be a ... because ...' and one way this job can help Oman in the future.

48.a: The teacher puts oo, ue and ew on three walls and says words (school, blue, new, food, glue, crew); pupils point to the right wall. The last words: blue sea, dhow crew!

49.a: The teacher plays 'Ranger says' in a park in Oman: 'You must put litter in the bin' (pupils mime it), 'You mustn't shout' (pupils freeze); out pupils become rangers.

50.a: Pupils give a definition of an Omani thing (You drink it with dates. It's hot and brown.) and the class writes the word in the air: coffee! Then a new pupil gives one.

51.a: A pupil mimes helping a family member like Shahad (fixing a bike with dad, carrying dates for grandma); the class says 'She's helping her dad. She's fixing a bike.'

52.a: A pupil mimes an illness (a cough, a headache); the class gives advice with should/shouldn't (You should drink water. You should eat dates, not sweets.).

53.a: Pairs act visiting a sick friend at home, as Omani families do: they bring dates, ask 'What's the matter?' and give advice with you should / you shouldn't.

0.a: A pupil mimes a free-time activity they do at the weekend (visiting grandparents, going to the beach); the class asks 'Do you ... on Friday?' until they guess.

1.a: Pupils make a chain about a day: 'After I wake up, I help my mum.' The next pupil repeats and adds a new action with before, after or when.

2.a: The teacher describes an Omani grandfather (He's got a white beard and short dark hair. He's wearing a kumma.); pupils draw him in one minute and compare pictures.

3.a: The teacher acts a quick situation (serving coffee to a guest, pushing in a queue); pupils show thumbs up or down and say 'That's polite!' 'That's rude!' 'He's kind!'

4.a: Volunteers show a ten-second talent (a tongue twister, a riddle, a line of an Omani song); the class describes them with adjectives: 'She's confident! He's funny!'

5.a: Groups compare three Omani places or dishes with more/most, better/best (Salalah is greener than Muscat. Shuwa is the best!) and the class votes for the best sentence.

6.a: Pupils walk and ask 'Are you good at baking bread / swimming / drawing a dhow?' and find someone for each; then they report one classmate's talent.

7.a: Pairs act a short welcome in an Omani home: greet the guest, offer coffee and dates, say please and thank you; the class names the good manners they saw.

8.a: Pairs role-play a new student at school: 'Who's that girl? What's she like? She seems friendly!' then walk over and welcome her kindly to the class.

9.a: Three volunteers are suspects; each says where they were at break. The class asks questions to find who ate all the dates, then says why honesty is important.

10.a: A pupil describes a family member's appearance and personality (She's kind and she's got grey hair.) and the class guesses the relative: grandma? aunt?

11.a: Pupils pass a ball; the holder makes a sentence with a personality adjective or a hobby (My friend is kind. He's good at football.). The last sentence: Omanis are friendly!

12.a: A volunteer is a tourist visiting Oman; the class asks personal questions (Where do you live? What's your favourite Omani food?) and the tourist answers.

13.a: The teacher asks 'Which is more fun: a wadi or a beach?'; pupils move to one side of the room and give a reason with because. More questions follow.

14.a: Groups act sharing one big dish with guests, as Omani families do, using story words (bowl, soup, more, enough); the class says if everyone got enough.

15.a: The teacher says technology words; pupils stand up for old technology (letter, telephone, CD player) and sit for new (tablet, email), then say how technology helps them study.

16.a: Pairs act calling grandma to invite her to Eid lunch, first on an old telephone, then on a mobile phone; the class says which phone is better and why.

17.a: Groups build a funny story in the past simple about a trip to a wadi; each pupil adds one sentence (We went to the wadi. We swam. Then a goat ate our lunch!).

18.a: Pairs make sentences comparing childhoods (My grandfather could climb a palm tree when he was ten. I couldn't!) and share the most surprising one.

19.a: A pupil plays a guide at a museum in Oman: 'Here you can see old khanjars and pots.' Visitors ask 'Can I take photos? What can I do here?'

20.a: The teacher throws a ball; the catcher asks an information question about a place in Oman (What time does Nizwa Fort open? How much is a ticket?) and another pupil answers.

21.a: Groups have one minute to brainstorm things to make from old cardboard boxes (a model fort, a dhow, a desk tidy) and present their best idea to keep Oman clean.

22.a: A pupil thinks of a place in Oman they visited; the class asks past simple questions (Did you see the sea? Did you eat fish?) and guesses the place.

23.a: Teams race to change the teacher's sentence into the past (Grandpa rides a camel. Grandpa rode a camel.), then say one thing that has changed in Oman.

24.a: Groups make a set of four words about Oman with one odd word (dates, halwa, coffee, bus); other groups say which is different: 'This one is different because ...'

25.a: Pupils walk and ask 'Could you swim when you were six? Could you make Omani bread?' and find a classmate for each, then report the funniest answer.
