26.a: The teacher reads situations (invite grandma to lunch, thank a teacher); pupils move to the 'letter' or 'email' side and give a reason.

27.a: Pupils are sailors on a dhow at night, as Omani sailors who used the stars to find their way; the teacher calls space words and pupils act them (a rocket, a comet, a star).

28.a: Pairs are astronauts on the space station looking down at Oman; each says one sentence with story words (I can see the blue sea and the desert of Oman!).

29.a: The teacher says a situation (Guests are at the door! It's very hot!); pupils act and answer with will (I'll make the coffee! I'll open the window!).

30.a: The teacher auctions pretend souq items (a model dhow, a silver box); pupils bid with big numbers (five hundred thousand baisa!) and the highest correct bid wins.

31.a: Pairs act old traders at a port in Dhofar: a buyer and a seller of frankincense ask and answer about how it is used and where it grows.

32.a: A pupil spells the name of a wilaya in Oman letter by letter (N-I-Z-W-A); the first pupil to say it correctly spells the next one.

33.a: The class plays a memory chain: 'On my trip to space I'll take dates.' The next pupil repeats and adds an item, and so on around the group.

34.a: Pupils act an astronaut on a live call from the space station to a school in Oman, saying one thing they will do today and one thing they miss about Oman.

35.a: Pairs make one prediction with will/won't about their town in the year 2040 (There will be more trees. People won't drop litter.) and the class claps for the best one.

36.a: The teacher draws three quick pictures (a boy on an Omani beach at night, a telescope, a comet); groups tell the story with one sentence each.

37.a: A pupil stands with their back to the board; the teacher writes a space word and the class gives clues. The last word is Oman, and the class gives clues about our country.

38.a: The teacher says race situations (He helps a friend who falls. She pushes to win.); pupils jump right for fair and left for unfair and say why.

39.a: The teacher says an item (fish, a silver ring, frankincense, tomatoes) and teams shout the shop (the fishmonger's! the jeweller's!) for points.

40.a: Pairs act finding a lost wallet in a shop and returning it: 'Excuse me, I found this in the toy shop.' The class says which honest words they heard.

41.a: The teacher says a sentence with a gap (Nizwa is a town ___ there is a big fort.); pupils show the answer with actions: hands on head for who, point for which, arms wide for where.

42.a: Pupils make a chain: 'At home I have to help my mum. I don't have to cook.' The next pupil repeats and adds a new sentence with have to / don't have to.

43.a: Groups make a two-line radio advert for a corner shop in their village selling Omani products (Come to Saif's shop! We sell fresh dates!) and perform it.

44.a: The teacher holds a pretend gift (a small dhow model); pupils ask 'How much is it?' and guess in rials; the teacher says 'more' or 'less' until someone is right.

45.a: Pairs think of one sentence to reply to the email, inviting the writer to visit Oman (Come to Oman! We will show you the souq.) and share it with the class.

46.a: The teacher says shop names (the butcher's, Ali's shop, shoes, the baker's); pupils draw an apostrophe in the air when it is needed, then name a favourite shop in their town.

47.a: The class plays: 'I went to the souq and I bought fish at the fishmonger's.' Each pupil repeats the list and adds a new shop and item.

48.a: The teacher tells a short story about a trip to Sur to see the dhow builders and stops before key words; pupils shout the missing word.

49.a: A pupil describes an Omani thing using who, which or where but without saying its name (It's a place where you can buy spices.); the class guesses: the souq!

50.a: Groups decide what Rosie could buy for her grandma at an Omani souq with only five rials, using have to and which (She has to find a gift which is cheap.).

51.a: Pupils each get one word and line up to make a correct sentence (Nizwa is a town which has a famous fort.); the class reads it together.

52.a: Pupils throw a ball; the catcher answers the suggestion (Good idea!) and makes a new one about a place in Oman (Why don't we visit the beach?).

53.a: Pupils act the planets moving around a pupil who is the Sun; when the teacher says 'Earth', everyone stops and says why we can live on Earth and one way to protect it.

54.a: Pupils pretend to lie on the sand in an Omani desert at night; each points up and says a fact from their fact file (Look! I can see Mars. It's red.).

0.a: Groups suggest one fun Omani topic for the magazine cover (turtles at Ras al Jinz, Muttrah Souq, Omani food) and the class votes for the best one.

1.a: The teacher says an adjective (brave, energetic, chatty, kind); pupils freeze as a statue. Finish by naming Omani people we admire (a brave fisherman, a kind neighbour).

2.a: The teacher calls sports; pupils jump for go, clap for play and stamp for do (go swimming, play football, do karate, go camel racing).

3.a: Pupils line up from 'never' to 'every day' to show how often they do an activity (go to the beach, play football, eat dates) and say a sentence.

4.a: A pupil mimes an action; the class says two sentences: 'He's eating dates now. He usually eats dates with coffee.' Then the pupil chooses the next mime.

5.a: Groups brainstorm fun things to do with family in Oman without Wi-Fi (play traditional games, visit grandparents, walk in a wadi) and share their best idea.

6.a: The teacher says hobbies (do photography, collect cards, make pottery); pupils walk to the 'love', 'like' or 'hate' wall and say a sentence with a state verb.

7.a: Groups invent a new sport that mixes an Omani tradition with a modern sport (camel volleyball!) and explain it in two sentences.

8.a: The teacher suggests 'Let's go to the beach!'; everyone shouts 'Yes, let's!' and mimes. A volunteer makes the next suggestion about a place in Oman.

9.a: The teacher says a sentence about Oman with a nonsense word (We climbed to the top of the high blorp.); pupils use the context to guess the real word.

10.a: Pairs write the most interesting question to ask an Omani sports star or fisherman; the class votes for the best question and says why it is good.

11.a: Pupils write a one-line comment about the best hobby to do in Oman on paper, stick it on the wall and walk around to read and tick their favourite.

12.a: Pairs say where in Oman is the best place to take photos and why (You should take photos at the fort because it's very old.).

13.a: Pupils 'volley' an imaginary ball with a question (Can you swim in the sea?); the catcher answers 'Yes, I can!' or 'No, I can't' and asks the next one.

14.a: A pupil mimes a park hobby; the class guesses (She's flying a kite!). Finish with one rule for keeping our parks in Oman clean.

15.a: Pairs invent a new app to help visitors in Oman (to find forts, souqs or beaches), give it a name and say one sentence about what it does.

16.a: Pairs act a short technology problem (My laptop won't turn on!) with a worried voice; the partner helps kindly. The class claps for the best feelings.

17.a: Pairs say a sentence about life in old Oman with had to or couldn't (People had to get water from the falaj.); the class shows thumbs up if they agree.

18.a: Groups make a two-line rhyme about Oman (The sea is blue, the sky is too; Oman, Oman, we all love you!) and perform it.

19.a: Two pupils mime technology actions (upload a photo, type a message); the class compares them with comparative adverbs (Ali types faster than Salim.).

20.a: In pairs, one pupil closes their eyes and the partner guides them carefully to the door with clear words, showing kindness and respect for others.

21.a: Pairs act a grandpa asking his grandson for help with his phone; the grandson answers politely (Of course, Grandpa! Could you give me your phone?).

22.a: Pairs give a two-sentence spoken review of a place in Oman with a good and a bad point (The souq is exciting but it's crowded.).

23.a: The teacher names Omani things (shuwa, a camel ride, the beach); pupils show one to five fingers and give a reason with an adjective or an adverb.

24.a: The teacher reads statements (Tablets help us learn faster. Young Omanis can make great apps.); pupils walk to 'agree' or 'disagree' and give a reason.

25.a: A pupil writes a unit word with a finger on a partner's back; the partner says and spells it. The last word is Oman.

26.a: A pupil goes out; the class hides a pretend phone. The pupil returns and finds it with clues (It's under the desk.), then says why we return lost things.

27.a: A pupil is the Animal App; the class asks about Omani animals (Which is faster, a falcon or a camel?) and the app answers with comparatives.

28.a: A pupil draws an Omani thing or a unit word on the board; teams guess it and give a definition.

29.a: Pupils walk in a circle; the teacher calls 'Past!' or 'Now!' with a topic (travel, water, light); a pupil says a sentence with had to / can about life in Oman.
Pairs act commentators at an Omani camel race, comparing the camels (This camel runs faster than that one! It's running more slowly now!).

30.a: Groups make a castle, a harbour or a stadium with their bodies; the class guesses and names a place in Oman with one (There's a fort in Bahla.).

31.a: The teacher says 'I'm looking for a place where you can swim.'; pupils name the place (the sports centre!) and give the next clue with where, who or that.

32.a: The teacher throws a ball with a clue to finish (National Day is a day when ... / A potter is a person who ...); the catcher completes it with the right pronoun.

33.a: The teacher hides a paper 'painting'; teams ask yes/no questions (Is it near the window?) to find it, then say why museums protect our heritage.

34.a: Pupils mime a long action (painting the wall of a fort); the teacher claps and pupils say 'I was painting the wall when the teacher clapped.'

35.a: A pupil acts a guide from long ago in an old Omani town, telling visitors about the fort and the falaj; visitors ask questions.

36.a: Desks become shops in a mall; pupils give a volunteer directions (Go up the stairs and turn left.) to the gift shop that sells Omani frankincense.

37.a: Groups invent a new ending for the story set in an Omani wadi and tell it in three sentences; the class votes for the best one.

38.a: The teacher calls a character, a place and a problem (a fisherman, Sur, a storm); groups tell a three-sentence story with these features.

39.a: Pupils make a chain: 'I visited a fort where I saw old cannons.' The next pupil repeats and adds a new place or thing with a relative pronoun.

40.a: Groups design a new building for their town that mixes modern and Omani style (wooden doors, arches) and describe it in two sentences.

41.a: The teacher makes a sound (a plane, a fire engine); pupils name the place (the airport!) and give directions to it from the school in their wilaya.

42.a: The teacher whispers a technology word to each pupil; they run to the right group (internet, machines, home). Then the class decides: is a falaj old technology?

0.a: Groups write a catchy magazine headline about an Omani place or event (Turtles Return to Ras al Jinz!) and the class votes for the best.

1.a: A pupil gives three clues as an Omani place in the first person (I'm very old. I'm in Nizwa. Visitors climb my tower.); the class guesses it.

2.a: Pairs act a quick audition at the Royal Opera House Muscat: one is a judge, the other a singer, dancer or magician who explains what they do.

3.a: The teacher reads facts and riddles; pupils react with the right expression: 'That's cool!' for an Omani fact, 'I've no idea!' for a hard riddle, 'I get it!' after the answer.

4.a: The teacher says time expressions (2020, three years, National Day, a long time); pupils clap once for since and twice for for, then make a sentence.

5.a: A pupil says a made-up diary line about a day in Muscat (Today we walked along the Corniche and ate halwa.); the class asks questions about the day.

6.a: Pupils walk and ask 'What are you doing on Friday?' (I'm visiting a park.) and find a classmate who is free, then report their plans.

7.a: Groups make a ten-second frozen performance (a folk dance, an acrobat, a singer); the class guesses the kind of performance.

8.a: The teacher is a ticket seller at a fort; each team sends a leader to buy tickets politely for their 'family' (two adults, three children); the class checks the price.

9.a: Groups make a three-line spoken advert for an activity in Oman (Come and see dolphins in Muscat! Book now!) and perform it with energy.

10.a: Groups invent a catchy slogan with an imperative verb (Visit…, Relax…, Explore…) for a place in Oman such as Nizwa Fort or Wadi Shab and shout it like a radio advert; the class claps for the best one.

11.a: Students walk around; at each clap they tell the nearest classmate one sentence with since or for about a favourite place in their wilaya (I have known this wadi for three years).

12.a: Pairs play quick ping-pong: one says a line about a trip to an Omani souq (Shall we buy some halwa?) and the partner fires back the best reply (Good idea! / Sorry, I can't.); then they swap.

13.a: A volunteer secretly chooses a job at an Omani place (a guide at Bahla Fort, a fisherman in Sur); the class asks How long have you…? and other questions and guesses the job.

14.a: Pairs plan a mini tour of their own town with three times and places (At ten o'clock we visit the souq…) and read it aloud like tour guides; the class guesses the town.
The class tosses a soft ball; the catcher uses one new word from the story in a sentence about a place in Oman they would show a visitor, then throws the ball on.
Students mime a job they would like to do to serve Oman (doctor, pilot, teacher, engineer); the class asks Are you a…? and the actor says one way the job helps people.

15.a: Students stand in a circle and pass a ball; the catcher says one Unit 1 word they now know well and one learning goal, just as Oman Vision 2040 sets goals for a better future.

16.a: The class plays Simon says with body parts (Simon says flap your wings, wave your tail); in the last round students act out an animal of Oman (camel, falcon, turtle) and name one body part.

17.a: Pairs act a short walk in a wadi or on a beach; one spots an animal (a snake, a baby turtle) and they use Watch out! / Wow! It's so cute! and say why we leave wild animals alone.

18.a: Volunteers mime using a traditional Omani object (a coffee pot, a khanjar, a fishing net); the class deduces with It might be…, It can't be…, It must be… and the actor reveals the answer.
Groups give one clue at a time about a famous place in Oman (It has thick walls… It's very old…); the class deduces with It might be… / It must be… until they guess the place.

19.a: Groups make a frozen picture of a scene from the platypus tale; the class guesses the scene, then says one way we welcome people who are different, as Omanis welcome guests.

20.a: The class builds a clapping chain of first conditional sentences about Oman's beaches: If we leave rubbish, turtles will eat it. If turtles eat it, they will… Each student adds one link.
One student mimes an animal verb (sting, dive, hatch, climb); the team guesses it and makes a first conditional sentence, e.g. If you go to Ras al Jinz at night, you might see turtles hatch.

21.a: Pairs role-play a reporter interviewing an Arabian oryx: Where do you live? What do you look like? The oryx answers with facts from the text and says why people in Oman protect it.

22.a: The teacher names animals and Omani things (camels, dates, the beach, sand); students stand tall for I love it or crouch for I can't stand it, say the expression and clap the word stress.

23.a: Pairs say three fact-file headings with short facts about an animal of Oman, such as the green turtle or the Arabian leopard (Habitat: mountains; Body: spotted fur); the class guesses the animal.

24.a: Students pass a ball; the catcher says a fact-file heading (Habitat, Food, Size, Special features) and a matching fact about a wild animal of Oman, e.g. Habitat: the Arabian tahr lives in the mountains.

25.a: Pairs make a first conditional promise to protect animals in Oman (If we keep the beach clean, the turtles will be safe) and act it with gestures; the class votes for the best promise.

26.a: The teacher says three quick sentences about Oman, one wrong (A dhow is a kind of plane); teams race to find the wrong option and prove it: It's wrong because…, just like in the exam.

27.a: Students move around like animals while the class hums; when the humming stops they freeze, and classmates make deductions (She might be a camel; He must be a falcon!).

28.a: Students take turns as a desert guide in Wahiba Sands giving a warning with if (If you touch a scorpion, it will sting you!); the group acts out the warning and thanks the guide.
The teacher describes clues on a family desert trip in Oman (big round footprints near the tent); students stand for must or crouch for might and say the deduction: It must be a camel!
Pairs mime an animal you can see in a garden or park in Oman (a bird, a lizard, a butterfly), showing its body parts; the partner guesses and names the parts, then says how we care for gardens.

29.a: The teacher says words from Units 1–2 (fort, guide, falcon, souq, teacher, oryx); students clap once for a place, twice for a job and stamp for an animal, then give an Omani example of each.

30.a: Pairs choose a place in Oman (Jebel Shams, a beach in Sur, Salalah in the khareef) and mime packing three items from the lesson; the class guesses the items and the place.

31.a: Groups plan a family picnic in a wadi: each offers to bring an item, others reply Good plan! or Of course!, and one student reminds everyone to take the rubbish home.

32.a: The teacher says a plan with going to (We're going to visit Nizwa souq tomorrow) and then a surprise (Oh no, it's raining!); students react with will (I'll take an umbrella).

33.a: Pairs act an astronaut calling home from the Moon using phrasal verbs (put on my helmet, take off, switch off) and saying one thing from Oman they miss, like Mum's harees or the beach.

34.a: A student mimes a travel verb (take off, land, get on, check in); the class says the verb and makes a timetable sentence about a trip in Oman (The bus to Sur leaves at eight o'clock).

35.a: The class plays Would you rather…: students move left or right for train or dhow, desert or mountains, fast or slow, and give a reason; the dhow side says why dhows are part of Oman's heritage.

36.a: The teacher names future events (a class trip to the beach, National Day celebrations, visiting grandparents for Eid); students make faces and say a Say it! expression about how they feel.

37.a: The teacher says four items for a trip to a desert camp (water, sunhat, snow boots, torch); pairs shout the odd one out and explain why, then add one good-manners rule for the trip.

38.a: Pairs say a one-line email from a place in Oman with two adjectives (Dear Sara, Sur is beautiful and the dhows are amazing!); the class claps for the best adjectives.

39.a: Pairs role-play a tourist and an Omani travel agent; the agent suggests a place with going to, will and the Present simple (The tour starts at nine. You'll love Nizwa Fort!).

40.a: Groups invent a short notice that keeps a public place in Oman clean or safe (Please put rubbish in the bins); they read it aloud and the class guesses where it would be.

41.a: The class pretends to be on a long bus journey across Oman and plays I spy (something beginning with F – a fort!); each guesser then says one place they are going to visit.

42.a: Students make clock hands with their arms for times the teacher says (quarter past seven, half past two); then the teacher names a season and students say what it is like in Oman.

43.a: Four corners become a Carroll diagram (needs light / sound); the teacher names places like a souq, a football stadium or a fort museum, students run to a corner and say: It needs light but doesn't need sound.

44.a: The teacher names traditional Omani jobs (potter in Bahla, fisherman, dhow builder, silversmith); students show thumbs up for makes heat and wave for makes movement, then say the sentence.

0.a: Groups invent a WOW! Magazine headline about something special in Oman (Meet the Dhow Builders of Sur!) and say one reason readers will love it; the class votes for the best cover story.

1.a: Students mingle and use question words to find someone who has visited a fort, likes Omani halwa, can name a wilaya in Dhofar or has a falaj in their village; they report one answer.

2.a: Students mime environment phrases (recycle plastic, save water, pick up litter, plant trees); the class guesses the phrase and says how it can keep Oman's beaches and wadis clean.

3.a: The teacher says energy-saving ideas for an Omani home or school (Switch off the AC when you leave!); the class answers with Brilliant!, I know! or Me too! with the right intonation and a gesture.

4.a: The teacher names a public place in Oman (a souq, a wadi, a fort museum, a park); teams race to make a polite rule with must, mustn't, should or needn't, e.g. You mustn't leave litter in the wadi.
A volunteer mimes wasting water (brushing teeth with the tap on); the class gives advice with should, mustn't or need to and remembers that falaj water is precious in Oman.

5.a: The teacher calls out get phrasal verbs (get under, get out, get onto, get up); students mime them fast, then pairs say one way neighbours in Oman help each other after a storm.

6.a: Pairs act Omani TV weather reporters warning about a sandstorm or heavy rain with should advice (You shouldn't cross a flooded wadi!); the class acts the weather with sound effects.
Teams whisper a short command or question down a line (Help your grandmother!); the last student reports it with reported speech (She told me to help my grandmother); correct reports score.

7.a: Students speak as an animal in danger (I live in the Hajar Mountains. I have short horns.) and say why life is hard; the class guesses the animal, such as the Arabian tahr.
Each group has 30 seconds to sell its best idea to help its animal, adding how their school or wilaya could join in; the class votes for the most convincing pitch.

8.a: A student plays a tourist with a problem (I only have one day in Oman!); classmates give advice with I think you should…, Perhaps you ought to… and Why don't you…? and the tourist picks the best.

9.a: The teacher names everyday items (plastic bag, water bottle, straw); students make an action for refuse, reuse or recycle and say a sentence about keeping Oman's beaches and turtles safe.

10.a: The class does a quick hands-up survey on favourite Omani dishes (shuwa, harees, majboos); pairs then make contrast sentences: Ten students chose shuwa, while five chose harees. However, …

11.a: Pairs play word tennis with Unit 1 words (recycle, flood, should, climate change); a player who stops loses the point, and winners finish with one thing they will do for a cleaner Oman.

12.a: Groups tell the story of a green turtle swimming back to a beach in Oman to lay eggs, one sentence each with sound effects, and end with one rule for visitors to turtle beaches.

13.a: Students mime advice an older family member gave them while the class guesses, then report it: My grandfather told me to respect guests. My mother said I should help neighbours.

14.a: Pairs act a volunteer and a vet at a rescue centre after a storm, using news, damage, injured and rescue centre; they end by thanking each other for helping the community.

15.a: Students freeze as an extreme sport; the class guesses it and names a place in Oman to try it (sandboarding in Wahiba Sands, diving near the Daymaniyat Islands, hiking in Wadi Shab).
Corners are I've done it, I'd like to try it, Maybe and Never; the teacher names a sport and a place in Oman (kayaking in Musandam); students move and give a reason.

16.a: The teacher reads statements (Sandboarding is dangerous; Every visitor should try Omani coffee); students stand on an agree–disagree line and answer with I suppose so., Not really. or I told you so!

17.a: Pairs act an Omani welcome: the host offers dates and coffee saying Help yourselves! and Make yourself at home!; guests reply with reflexive pronouns (We made this ourselves? Thank you!).
In a circle, each student says one thing they did by themselves to help family or neighbours (I fixed my brother's bike myself); a classmate reports it with himself or herself.

18.a: Teams race to describe Omani things with compound adjectives (a well-known fort, sun-dried dates, world-famous frankincense, an old-fashioned dhow); each correct one scores a point.

19.a: A student thinks of a place in Oman; the class asks yes/no questions with geography words (Is it near a bay? Is it in the north? Is there a valley?) until someone guesses it.
The class builds a story about a trip to Jebel Akhdar, each student adding a sentence with after + Past perfect (After we had packed the car, we drove up the mountain).

20.a: Groups invent a fun new sport for an Omani beach or desert, give it a name and two rules and mime it; the class votes for the sport they would most like to try.
Pairs act as sports commentators giving an exciting thirty-second commentary on a traditional race in Oman, such as a dhow race or a camel race; the class cheers and claps.

21.a: Pairs ask each other quick Would you rather…? questions about Oman (visit Wadi Shab or Jebel Shams? eat harees or shuwa?) and answer with I'd prefer to… / I'd rather… and a reason.
In a circle, each student says an I'd rather… sentence about an Omani choice (I'd rather visit a fort than a mall) and claps the stressed words; the class echoes with the same rhythm.

22.a: The teacher says a plain sentence (Muttrah Souq is nice); teams race to make it persuasive with strong adjectives (Muttrah Souq is amazing and unforgettable!); the best version wins a point.

23.a: Groups perform a twenty-second radio advert for an extreme sport in Oman that starts with a question (Do you love speed? Try sandboarding in Wahiba Sands!) and ends with an exciting sentence.

24.a: The teacher says a letter; students write a sport, a geography word and a place in Oman with that letter; the first to finish shouts Stop the bus! and reads the words aloud.

25.a: Students sit in a pretend campfire circle and give an opinion about camping in Oman (I think camping in the desert is more exciting because…) plus one rule to keep the campsite clean.

26.a: The class tells an adventure story about a day in an Omani wadi one word at a time; whenever a Past perfect or reflexive pronoun appears, everyone claps.

27.a: A student plays a sandboarding instructor giving safety instructions (Put on your goggles! Check your knee pads!); the class mimes, then the instructor names one ancient place in Oman to visit.

28.a: The teacher tells a short story about a falcon in the Omani mountains using the new words; students do an action each time they hear one (flap, nest hands, proud chest, equipment mime).

29.a: Pairs role-play a customer and a seller in an Omani souq using the shopping words (queue, receipt, bank card, till, sale) and finish with a polite thank you and a smile.

30.a: The teacher says funny shopping sentences (I'll buy a camel online!); pairs react fast with No chance!, I'm only kidding! or That's true.; the last one is: We should buy from local craftspeople.

31.a: The class makes a chain of conditionals about saving money: If I save money, I'll buy a gift for my grandmother. If I buy a gift, she'll be happy… Each student adds one link.

32.a: Pairs make a two-line rhyme about a place in Oman (Would you like to see the sea / at Sur with me?) and perform it; the class claps the rhyme.

33.a: Students sit on an imaginary magic carpet and each says a second conditional wish about Oman (If I had a magic carpet, I'd fly over the Hajar Mountains); others mime the flight.

34.a: Students give three clues about an item sold in an Omani souq (frankincense, halwa, pottery, silver jewellery) without saying its name; the class guesses with If I visited the souq, I'd buy…

35.a: The teacher says a funny problem (My new dishdasha is too long!); pairs instantly act a polite complaint and a helpful shop assistant's solution using the Say it! phrases.

36.a: The teacher reads email openings and endings; students stand for formal and sit for informal, then each says a friendly welcome line to a pen friend coming to visit Oman.

37.a: Pairs ask each other three quick questions about their town (Where can we eat? What can we buy?); the partner answers all three in a friendly informal style and invites the friend to visit.

38.a: The teacher reads situations (You get money for Eid); students move to the Spend or the Save side and give a conditional reason; one choice is to give some to help others.

39.a: Groups imagine an Omani souq in the future, in the spirit of Oman Vision 2040, and give two predictions with will (People will pay with their phones; old crafts will still be sold).

40.a: A volunteer pretends to be an Omani author at a book signing; classmates ask questions with the new words (Will you sign my book? Is this bookmark free?) and one asks If you…, would you…?

41.a: Pairs play higher or lower with big numbers (Is it six hundred and fifty?), pretending to guess how many dates a farm picked for guests; correct use of and with hundred scores a point.

42.a: Students stand in a line and each adds one cause-and-effect link with because, so or due to: We drop litter → it goes into the sea → turtles eat it → … ; the last student gives a solution.

43.a: Pairs play ping-pong: one gives a cause about nature in Oman (Families plant trees in their village), the partner adds the effect with so or because of; the longest rally wins.

0.a: Pairs say a two-sentence social media post about a weekend in Oman using a, an and the (I visited an old fort. The fort had a great view!) without naming the place; the class guesses it.
Students mime a holiday activity they did in Oman; classmates ask past simple questions (Did you go camping in the desert? Did you swim in a wadi?) until they guess it.
Pairs act a TV reporter interviewing a classmate about their best moment (What happened? How did you feel?) and finish with: How did it make your family or school proud?

1.a: Students stand in a circle; one says an adjective about themselves or something about their Omani identity they are proud of (I'm friendly; I love our hospitality); everyone who shares it steps in.
Groups make a frozen photo of a scene from Omani life (a family drinking coffee with dates, a fisherman's boat, a falaj); the class describes the photo board scene and what it shows about identity.

2.a: A volunteer mimes a daily action (making Omani coffee, watering palm trees); the class says what he or she is doing now and what people usually do, e.g. He's making coffee. He usually makes it for guests.

3.a: In a circle, each student gives the next classmate a kind compliment with a positive personality adjective or collocation (Ahmed is generous; Mona is good at helping others), showing Omani respect.

4.a: The teacher names places in Oman (busy Muscat, a quiet mountain village, a beach at sunset, Salalah in the khareef); students show a face and say how the place makes them feel with an emotion adjective.
The teacher says a routine (visit my grandparents, eat dates, help at home); students stand on a line from never to always and say their sentence with the adverb in the right position.

5.a: Teams spell the name of a wilaya (Bahla, Sohar, Ibri, Sur) letter by letter, one student per letter; the last student says why someone should visit it, using because or for example.

6.a: The teacher says sentences about places in Oman (Jebel Shams is ___ cool in winter; Muttrah Souq is ___ busy); students raise one hand for quite or two for very and explain their choice.
The teacher says two short sentences about Oman (The souq is busy. I love it.); teams race to join them with and, but, or, because or so, then praise another team: I liked the way you…

7.a: Pairs role-play a teenager asking a grandparent to teach a traditional skill (making halwa, weaving, repairing a fishing net) using collocations like take a class and join a class.

8.a: The teacher says the first part of a collocation (keen…, good…, interested…); the class shouts the preposition, and a volunteer makes a sentence about an Omani hobby (I'm keen on fishing).
Pairs interview each other: How often do you help older people? What are you doing this week to help your family or neighbours?; they report one kind habit to the class.

9.a: Pairs play tense tennis: one says a time expression (every Friday, at the moment, never), the partner makes a correct sentence about Omani family life (Every Friday we visit my grandparents).

10.a: Pairs act a tourist and a local: the local explains the way to an Omani fort using only gestures, then says the same directions in English; the class guesses the directions first.
Students teach a partner how to say welcome in a language they know, then discuss in one sentence why welcoming visitors in many languages is part of Omani hospitality.

11.a: Pairs build stories about older generations: one says what a grandparent was doing (My grandfather was sailing his dhow), the partner adds a past simple event (when a big wave came).

12.a: The teacher reads sentences with a gap (My grandfather ___ me a story about the old souq); teams race to shout the right verb and preposition and get a point for each correct answer.

13.a: Pairs act a person and an animal from Oman (a camel, a falcon, a horse); the person communicates kindly with words and gestures and the class guesses the animal and gives one kind rule.
In a circle, each student starts a sentence with an -ing form about Oman (Protecting turtles is important; Visiting forts is fun) and the next student agrees or disagrees with a reason.

14.a: Pairs describe a well-known Omani scene from memory (a busy souq, the Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, a dhow at sea) using introduction, place and people; the class guesses the scene.

15.a: Students tell a two-sentence story with the past simple and past continuous; the class votes true or made up, then says why being honest online matters.
The teacher says an ordinary sentence (The view from Jebel Shams is very good); students upgrade it with a strong adjective and a big gesture (It's absolutely amazing!).

16.a: Pairs plan a phone-free Friday with their family using I'll and I'd (I'll visit my grandmother; I'd love to go to the beach); the class listens for each contraction and claps.

17.a: A student sits with their back to the board; the team describes the word written there (ancient, translate, protect) with Omani examples (Bahla Fort is very old) until the student guesses it.
Pairs act a short disagreement between friends (who borrowed the ball), then make peace kindly and retell what happened with the past simple and past continuous.

18.a: A student detective asks What were you doing at seven o'clock yesterday?; classmates answer with the past continuous, e.g. I was visiting my aunt; the detective spots who changed their story.

19.a: Groups imagine a virtual reality tour of an Omani place (walking through Nizwa Fort, diving at the Daymaniyat Islands) and present it in one exciting sentence; the class votes for the best tour.
The teacher names jobs (storyteller, tour guide at a fort, falaj engineer, coffee host at a wedding); students vote robot or human and give one reason that respects people's work.

20.a: Pairs act fortune tellers and make future predictions for each other with will and going to (You'll be an engineer who builds green cities in Oman); the partner reacts politely.
Students mingle to find someone who is visiting relatives this weekend, is going to help at home and will try a new Omani dish; they report one plan with the right future form.

21.a: The class plays Simon says with phrasal verbs (Simon says switch off the lights! Turn down the AC!); in the last round students say one way their family saves electricity at home.

22.a: A student describes buying a gift for a grandparent and mentions three items (I thought about a phone and a radio, but…); the class listens for the distractors and guesses the final choice.
The class gives advice to an imaginary new student in their Omani school, each using a different structure (You ought to…, Why don't you…?, How about…?, Shall I show you…?).

23.a: The teacher reads statements (Every family should plant a tree; Robots should work in shops); pairs answer with an agree or disagree phrase, saying something positive before disagreeing.

24.a: Groups invent a teen tech help idea for their wilaya (teaching grandparents video calls, helping at the library) and announce it in one sentence; the class votes for the most useful idea.
A volunteer plays Khalid choosing a community project; classmates give advice with should, ought to, could, why don't you and how about; Khalid chooses the best idea and says why.

25.a: Pairs role-play a video call between a doctor in Muscat and a patient in a far mountain village, using words from the video, and finish by saying why everyone should get good healthcare.

26.a: Pairs give a fun tour of an imaginary smart house in Oman using phrasal verbs and wordlist words (The lights come on when you walk in); the class asks one question per tour.
Groups give two ideas for a youth centre in their wilaya with will or going to (We're going to have a reading club); the class votes for the most helpful idea.

27.a: Pairs plan a class trip to clean a beach in Oman using offers and suggestions (Shall I bring the bags? Why don't we start early?) and share their best idea.

28.a: Teams make a relay of three sentences about Oman: the past (People travelled by dhow), the present (Now we…) and the future (Oman Vision 2040 will…); the fastest correct team wins.
